situation: Someone gained unauthorized access to my company's server and copied confidential files without permission.
it_act_sections: Section 43 (penalty for damage to computer system)
ipc_sections: Section 405 (criminal breach of trust) - legacy reference
explanation: Unauthorized access to a computer system or network and extraction of data without the owner's permission falls squarely under hacking provisions of the IT Act. Section 43 covers the civil penalty for unauthorized access, downloading, or copying of data, while Section 66 criminalizes the same act when done dishonestly or fraudulently, as defined with reference to Sections 24 and 25 of the Indian Penal Code/BNS (dishonesty and fraud).
punishment: Under Section 66 IT Act: imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh, or both. Section 43 allows for compensation to be paid to the affected party as determined by an adjudicating officer.

situation: A former employee logged into our company database using his old credentials after he was terminated and deleted important records.
it_act_sections: Section 66F (cyber terrorism, if scale is large) - not typically applicable here
ipc_sections: Section 405 (criminal breach of trust) - legacy reference
explanation: Accessing a computer resource without authorization (since access rights were revoked upon termination) and causing deletion or alteration of data constitutes both unauthorized access and data damage under Section 43, punishable under Section 66. The act may also amount to criminal breach of trust if the employee was in a position of trust regarding that data.
punishment: Imprisonment up to 3 years and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh under Section 66 IT Act. Additional civil liability for damages under Section 43.

situation: My Instagram account was hacked and the hacker changed my password and is now posting offensive content from my profile.
explanation: Gaining unauthorized control of someone's social media account by changing credentials constitutes hacking under Section 66, and using that account to post content while impersonating the victim attracts identity theft under Section 66C, since it involves fraudulent or dishonest use of another person's electronic signature, password, or unique identification.
punishment: Section 66: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh. Section 66C: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh.

situation: An unknown person accessed my email account and read my private conversations without my knowledge or consent.
it_act_sections: Section 72 (breach of confidentiality and privacy, if applicable to intermediary/authority)
ipc_sections: Section 354D (stalking, if repeated) - legacy reference, context dependent
bns_sections: Section 78 BNS (stalking, if repeated and applicable)
explanation: Unauthorized access to a private email account, even without altering data, is penalized under Section 43(a) for accessing a computer resource without permission, and criminally under Section 66. If the access is part of a pattern of monitoring, stalking provisions may also apply.
punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh under Section 66 IT Act.

situation: I found out someone installed a keylogger on my office laptop to monitor everything I type, including my banking passwords.
it_act_sections: Section 66C (identity theft, if passwords were used)
ipc_sections: Section 463/465 (forgery, if data is misused) - legacy reference
bns_sections: Section 336 BNS (forgery, if data is misused)
explanation: Installing a keylogger without consent to capture sensitive information like banking credentials qualifies as introducing a computer contaminant and unauthorized access under Section 43, punishable under Section 66. If captured credentials are subsequently used, Section 66C (identity theft) applies as well.
punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh under Section 66; up to 3 years and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh under Section 66C if credentials were misused.

situation: My neighbor uses my home WiFi without permission because I never changed the default password, but he hasn't caused any damage.
explanation: Even passive unauthorized use of a WiFi network without the owner's consent technically falls under Section 43(a) of the IT Act, which penalizes accessing or securing access to a computer, computer system, or network without permission. However, in practice, such low-harm cases are often resolved informally or treated as a civil matter (compensation under Section 43) rather than pursued criminally, since criminal liability under Section 66 requires dishonest or fraudulent intent.
punishment: Civil liability: compensation as determined by adjudicating officer under Section 43. Criminal liability under Section 66 only applies if dishonest/fraudulent intent is established, punishable up to 3 years and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh.

situation: A friend asked to borrow my laptop and I let him use it for an hour to check his email.
explanation: This is normal, consensual use of a device. There is no unauthorized access, no data theft, and no fraudulent intent. Since the laptop owner voluntarily permitted access for a lawful purpose, none of the elements of a cybercrime under the IT Act are present.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: I received a call from someone claiming to be from my bank asking for my OTP, and after I shared it, Rs. 50,000 was withdrawn from my account.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: This is a classic vishing (voice phishing) scam. The fraudster used the victim's OTP (a unique identification feature) to impersonate them and fraudulently access their bank account, which constitutes cheating by personation under Section 66D, alongside identity theft under Section 66C. The underlying cheating is also covered by BNS Section 318 (replacing IPC 420).
punishment: Section 66D: imprisonment up to 3 years and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh. Section 66C: imprisonment up to 3 years and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh. BNS 318 cheating: up to 7 years depending on the specific clause.

situation: I clicked on a link in an SMS that looked like it was from my bank, and it took me to a fake website that asked me to enter my net banking login details.
explanation: This is a phishing attack where a fake website was created to impersonate a legitimate bank in order to fraudulently obtain login credentials. This squarely falls under Section 66D, which deals with cheating by personation using a computer resource, and Section 66C for identity theft.
punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh under both Section 66C and 66D.

situation: Someone created a fake UPI payment request and tricked me into approving it, thinking I was receiving money, but instead Rs. 10,000 got deducted from my account.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: This is a 'collect request' UPI fraud, a well-known scam where victims are deceived into approving payment requests disguised as receipt requests. The deceptive use of a computer resource (UPI app) to defraud the victim attracts Section 66D of the IT Act along with cheating provisions under BNS.
punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh under Section 66D; cheating under BNS 318 can attract imprisonment up to 7 years depending on the clause invoked.

situation: I invested in a cryptocurrency scheme advertised on Telegram that promised guaranteed 30% monthly returns, and the platform vanished with my money after two months.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: Ponzi-style investment scams operated through online platforms involve cheating and criminal breach of trust facilitated through a computer resource, attracting Section 66D of the IT Act. Depending on the scale, such schemes may also attract the Prize Chits and Money Circulation Schemes (Banning) Act, 1978, and SEBI regulations if securities are involved.
punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh under Section 66D; cheating under BNS 318 can extend up to 7 years imprisonment depending on severity.

situation: I received an email saying I won a lottery of $1 million and need to pay a processing fee to claim it, and I'm worried this might be a scam.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: This describes a classic advance-fee/lottery scam sent via email. If the victim has not yet paid, this is an attempted offence; if money has already been transferred, it constitutes completed cheating via a computer resource under Section 66D of the IT Act.
punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh under Section 66D.

situation: My company received an email that looked like it was from our CEO asking the finance team to urgently wire Rs. 25 lakh to a new vendor account, and the finance manager complied before realizing it was fake.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: This is Business Email Compromise (BEC), where attackers impersonate a senior executive via a spoofed or compromised email account to defraud the organization. This involves both identity theft (Section 66C) and cheating by personation through a computer resource (Section 66D).
punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh under each of Section 66C and 66D; cheating under BNS 318 can extend up to 7 years depending on the amount and clause invoked.

situation: I paid my friend back Rs. 2,000 through Google Pay for dinner we had together last week.
explanation: This is a legitimate, voluntary digital payment between two consenting individuals for a genuine transaction. There is no deception, unauthorized access, or fraudulent intent involved, so no provision of the IT Act, IPC, or BNS is attracted.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: I sold my old phone to someone on OLX and we agreed on a price after some negotiation; the buyer paid the full agreed amount.
explanation: This is a legitimate online marketplace transaction completed honestly by both parties. There is no fraud, misrepresentation, or unauthorized computer access involved.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: An ex-colleague keeps sending me threatening and abusive messages on WhatsApp every day, even after I asked him to stop and blocked him on one number, since he keeps creating new numbers.
it_act_sections: Section 66A (struck down by Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal case, no longer applicable)
explanation: Repeated, unwanted contact through electronic communication despite a clear request to stop constitutes cyberstalking under Section 78 of the BNS (corresponding to erstwhile IPC Section 354D), and the threatening nature of the messages attracts criminal intimidation under Section 351 BNS. Note that Section 66A of the IT Act, which previously criminalized 'offensive' online messages, was struck down as unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) and cannot be invoked.
punishment: Stalking under BNS Section 78: up to 3 years for first conviction, up to 5 years for subsequent conviction, with fine. Criminal intimidation under BNS Section 351: up to 2 years, or fine, or both (up to 7 years if intimidation involves death/grievous hurt threats).

situation: Someone created a fake Facebook profile using my photos and is sending friend requests to my contacts and posting embarrassing content as if it were me.
explanation: Creating a fake profile using someone's photographs and identity to deceive others is identity theft under Section 66C and impersonation under Section 66D of the IT Act. If the content posted is damaging to reputation, defamation under BNS Section 356 also applies.
punishment: Section 66C/66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh each. Defamation under BNS Section 356: up to 2 years, or fine, or both, or community service.

situation: My ex-partner has been tracking my location through a shared app we used to use and shows up wherever I go, even though we broke up months ago and I've asked him to stop.
it_act_sections: Section 43 (unauthorized access/monitoring, if app access wasn't revoked properly)
Section 66E (violation of privacy, if location/images captured without consent)
explanation: Monitoring a person's location electronically without consent after a relationship has ended and despite being asked to stop is a clear case of cyberstalking under BNS Section 78. If location data is being accessed through an app the victim no longer knowingly consents to, it may also raise privacy violation concerns under Section 66E of the IT Act.
punishment: BNS Section 78: up to 3 years imprisonment for first offence (up to 5 years for repeat offence), along with fine.

situation: Students in my class created a WhatsApp group where they share morphed photos of me and make fun of my appearance, and the group has spread to other classes too.
it_act_sections: Section 66E (violation of privacy through morphed images)
explanation: Creating and circulating morphed images intended to humiliate someone violates their privacy under Section 66E of the IT Act and amounts to defamation under BNS Section 356. If the morphed images are sexually suggestive or obscene, Section 67 (publishing obscene material electronically) is also attracted, carrying significantly higher penalties.
punishment: Section 66E: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 2 lakh. Section 67 (if obscene): up to 3 years and fine up to Rs. 5 lakh for first conviction; up to 5 years and fine up to Rs. 10 lakh for subsequent conviction.

situation: My colleague keeps sending me unsolicited romantic messages on LinkedIn even though I've told her clearly I'm not interested and to stop contacting me.
explanation: Repeated, unwanted electronic contact of a personal/romantic nature after a clear refusal can constitute cyberstalking under BNS Section 78, which covers monitoring or contacting a person through the internet, email, or any other form of electronic communication despite a clear indication of disinterest.
punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment for first conviction, up to 5 years for subsequent conviction, along with fine, under BNS Section 78.

situation: I left a one-star review on a restaurant's Google listing because the food was bad and the service was slow.
explanation: Posting a genuine, honest review based on personal experience is a lawful exercise of consumer expression and free speech, not harassment or defamation. As long as the review reflects the reviewer's actual opinion and isn't maliciously false, no offence is made out.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out, provided the review is truthful and not maliciously fabricated.

situation: My brother and I argue over text messages sometimes about family matters, but it's just normal sibling disagreement.
explanation: Ordinary disagreements between family members conducted over text, without threats, intimidation, or harassment, do not meet the threshold for any cyber offence. Ordinary conflict is not criminalized.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: A photo studio I visited for a private photoshoot leaked my pictures online without my consent.
ipc_sections: Section 354C (voyeurism, if images were taken without knowledge/consent)
explanation: Publishing or transmitting images of a person's private parts or private moments without consent, capturing or circulating images in violation of a person's reasonable expectation of privacy, is squarely covered under Section 66E of the IT Act. If the images are sexually explicit, the much more severe Section 67A applies instead.
punishment: Section 66E: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 2 lakh. Section 67A (sexually explicit content): up to 5 years and fine up to Rs. 10 lakh for first conviction; up to 7 years and fine up to Rs. 10 lakh for subsequent conviction.

situation: I discovered that a mobile app I used for a personal loan accessed and downloaded my entire phone contact list and is now sending threatening messages to my contacts over my unpaid dues.
it_act_sections: Section 72A (disclosure of information in breach of lawful contract)
ipc_sections: Section 506 (criminal intimidation, for threats to contacts)
explanation: Unauthorized harvesting of personal data (contact lists) beyond what is reasonably necessary, and subsequent misuse of that data to harass third parties, violates Section 43 and Section 72A of the IT Act, which penalizes disclosure of personal information obtained while providing services under a lawful contract, without consent and with intent to cause wrongful loss. This is a recognized pattern in predatory loan-app harassment cases in India.
punishment: Section 72A: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh. Criminal intimidation under BNS 351: up to 2 years or fine or both.

situation: My ex-boyfriend is threatening to share my private photos with my family and friends if I don't get back together with him.
explanation: This is 'sextortion' - using the threat of releasing private/intimate images to coerce a person into compliance. This involves criminal intimidation and extortion under the BNS, combined with privacy violation under Section 66E of the IT Act, and Section 67A if the images are sexually explicit. This is treated as a serious offence by Indian cybercrime cells.
punishment: Section 67A: up to 5 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 10 lakh for first conviction. Extortion under BNS 308: up to 7 years imprisonment along with fine.

situation: An e-commerce website I shopped on suffered a data breach and my saved card details and address were leaked on the dark web.
it_act_sections: Section 43A (compensation for failure to protect data)
Section 72A (disclosure of information in breach of contract)
explanation: Under Section 43A of the IT Act, a body corporate that is negligent in implementing reasonable security practices to protect sensitive personal data is liable to pay compensation to the affected persons. If an identifiable individual within the company also disclosed the data dishonestly, Section 72A would apply to them personally. With the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 also in force, regulatory penalties from the Data Protection Board may apply to the company as well.
punishment: Section 43A: compensation as determined by adjudicating officer/courts, with no statutory cap on the amount. Section 72A: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh for the individual responsible.

situation: My doctor shared my medical test results with a pharmaceutical sales representative without asking me, and now I keep getting promotional calls about specific medications.
it_act_sections: Section 72A (disclosure of information in breach of lawful contract)
ipc_sections: Section 405 (criminal breach of trust, in some interpretations)
explanation: Sharing sensitive personal medical information obtained in the course of a professional/contractual relationship, without the patient's consent and for an unrelated commercial purpose, falls under Section 72A of the IT Act, which specifically targets unauthorized disclosure of personal information by a person providing services under a lawful contract.
punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh under Section 72A.

situation: I shared my own travel photos on my public Instagram account and tagged the locations I visited.
explanation: This is voluntary self-disclosure of one's own personal information on a public platform of one's own choosing. Since the person consented to and controlled the sharing of their own data, no privacy violation or cyber offence occurs.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: A man I matched with on a dating app sent me unsolicited explicit photos of himself without my consent.
it_act_sections: Section 67 (publishing/transmitting obscene material in electronic form)
explanation: Transmitting sexually explicit material electronically to a person without their consent constitutes an offence under Section 67A of the IT Act, which deals with publishing or transmitting material containing sexually explicit acts in electronic form. The lack of consent and unsolicited nature is key to establishing the offence.
punishment: Section 67A: up to 5 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 10 lakh for first conviction; up to 7 years and fine up to Rs. 10 lakh for subsequent conviction.

situation: I came across a website that appears to host sexually explicit images and videos of children.
it_act_sections: Section 67B (publishing/transmitting material depicting children in sexually explicit acts)
explanation: This describes Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM), which is among the most serious offences under Indian cyber law. Section 67B of the IT Act specifically criminalizes creating, browsing, downloading, advertising, promoting, exchanging, or distributing material depicting children in sexually explicit acts. This is prosecuted in conjunction with the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, and should be reported immediately to the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in) or the police.
punishment: Section 67B: up to 5 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 10 lakh for first conviction; up to 7 years and fine up to Rs. 10 lakh for subsequent conviction. POCSO penalties may be significantly higher and run concurrently.

situation: A YouTube channel posted a movie review video that included some non-explicit clips from the film for critique purposes.
explanation: Using short clips for the purpose of criticism, review, or commentary is generally protected as fair use/fair dealing under copyright law, and does not constitute obscenity or any cyber offence, provided the content itself is not obscene and does not infringe beyond the scope of fair dealing. This is a copyright/IP consideration rather than a cybercrime matter, unless the usage is excessive and constitutes piracy.
punishment: Not applicable as a cybercrime - potential copyright fair-dealing matter only, not criminal in nature if usage is limited and transformative.

situation: A former business partner posted false claims on LinkedIn that I embezzled company funds, which is completely untrue and has damaged my professional reputation.
it_act_sections: Section 66 (computer related offences, in relation to dissemination)
explanation: Publishing false and damaging statements about a person through an electronic medium with intent to harm their reputation constitutes defamation under BNS Section 356. Since the medium used is a computer resource (LinkedIn), the act may also be examined under the IT Act's general computer-related offence provisions if data manipulation or fake evidence is involved.
punishment: BNS Section 356: simple imprisonment up to 2 years, or fine, or both, or community service; defamation is also actionable as a civil wrong for damages.

situation: Someone is impersonating a well-known journalist on Twitter/X using a similar handle and profile photo, spreading false statements attributed to them.
explanation: Creating a fake account that impersonates a real, identifiable individual to deceive others into believing the statements are genuinely theirs constitutes identity theft (Section 66C) and cheating by personation (Section 66D) under the IT Act. If false statements attributed to the real person damage their reputation, defamation under BNS Section 356 also applies.
punishment: Section 66C/66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh each. Defamation: up to 2 years imprisonment or fine or both.

situation: A WhatsApp forward falsely claimed that a particular vaccine causes infertility, and it has been circulating widely in my community group, causing panic.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (if used to deceive for fraudulent gain) - typically not applicable for pure misinformation
bns_sections: Section 353 BNS (statements conducing to public mischief)
explanation: Spreading false information that is likely to cause public fear, alarm, or incite panic falls under BNS Section 353 (public mischief), regardless of the medium used. While the IT Act itself doesn't have a dedicated 'fake news' provision (Section 66A having been struck down), large-scale circulation of medical misinformation can attract action under the Disaster Management Act (during declared emergencies) and the IT Rules 2021's grievance mechanisms for platforms.
punishment: BNS Section 353: imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine, or both, depending on the specific clause and intent.

situation: I wrote a strongly worded but factual blog post criticizing a politician's voting record on a particular bill, using publicly available parliamentary records.
explanation: Fair criticism of a public figure's conduct in their official capacity, when based on true and publicly verifiable facts, is protected speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution and does not amount to defamation, since truth is a complete defense to a defamation claim and matters of public interest enjoy wider latitude for criticism.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out, as truthful criticism of public conduct is constitutionally protected.

situation: Someone used my Aadhaar and PAN details, which I never shared with them, to open a fraudulent loan account in my name.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
bns_sections: Section 340 BNS (using forged documents as genuine)
explanation: Fraudulent use of another person's unique identification documents (Aadhaar, PAN) to dishonestly obtain a financial benefit is a textbook case of identity theft under Section 66C, combined with cheating by personation under Section 66D. The use of forged or stolen identity documents also attracts forgery-related provisions under the BNS.
punishment: Section 66C: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh. Section 66D: up to 3 years and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh. Forgery offences under BNS can attract up to 7 years depending on the specific document type.

situation: I received a call where the caller ID showed my bank's official customer care number, but it turned out to be a scammer using caller ID spoofing technology.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: Caller ID spoofing to impersonate a legitimate institution and deceive the victim is a clear case of cheating by personation through a computer resource under Section 66D of the IT Act. This is increasingly common in India and is also addressed through TRAI/DoT regulations on telecom spoofing alongside criminal prosecution.
punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh under Section 66D.

situation: My company uses my real name on our official 'About Us' webpage along with my professional bio and photo, which I provided and approved.
explanation: This is the consensual, authorized use of one's own identity and information for a legitimate professional purpose, with the individual's knowledge and approval. There is no deception, impersonation, or unauthorized use involved.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: All the files on my company's systems got encrypted overnight, and a message appeared demanding Bitcoin payment to restore access.
it_act_sections: Section 66F (cyber terrorism, if scale/target qualifies as critical infrastructure)
explanation: This describes a ransomware attack, which involves introducing a computer contaminant (malicious encryption software) under Section 43(c), causing damage to a computer system under Section 66, and extorting payment under threat, which constitutes extortion under BNS Section 308. If the attack targets critical infrastructure (banking, healthcare, government systems) with intent to threaten the unity, integrity, or security of India, it could escalate to cyber terrorism under Section 66F, which is far more severe.
punishment: Section 66: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh. Extortion under BNS 308: up to 7 years imprisonment. Section 66F (cyber terrorism): imprisonment for life, if applicable.

situation: I downloaded a cracked version of a paid software from a torrent site and it ended up infecting my personal laptop with a virus that deleted my files.
it_act_sections: Section 43 (introduction of computer contaminant, though self-inflicted in this case complicates victim/perpetrator analysis)
explanation: While the user is technically the victim of the malware (their own files were damaged), it's worth noting that downloading pirated/cracked software itself is a separate copyright infringement issue under the Copyright Act, 1957. As the victim of the virus infection, the user could report this to a cybercrime cell, though attributing the attack to a specific perpetrator (the torrent uploader) for prosecution purposes can be difficult.
punishment: If a specific perpetrator who knowingly distributed the contaminant is identified: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh under Section 66. The user's own act of downloading pirated software may separately attract civil liability under the Copyright Act.

situation: I run antivirus software on my computer regularly as a precaution, and it occasionally flags and removes minor threats.
explanation: Running antivirus software for legitimate protection of one's own device is a standard cybersecurity practice, not a cyber offence. This is a defensive, lawful action.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: I ordered a smartphone from a website that looked legitimate, paid online, but received an empty box, and now the website is no longer reachable.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: This describes a fraudulent e-commerce scheme where a fake or shell website was set up to dishonestly induce payment without delivering genuine goods, which is cheating committed via a computer resource under Section 66D of the IT Act, combined with cheating provisions under BNS Section 318.
punishment: Section 66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh. BNS 318 (cheating): up to 7 years depending on the specific clause invoked, especially if it involves knowledge that delivery was never intended.

situation: I bought a laptop online and it arrived two days later than the promised delivery date due to a courier delay.
explanation: A delayed delivery due to logistical issues, without any intent to deceive or defraud, is a service deficiency matter governed by consumer protection law (Consumer Protection Act, 2019), not a criminal cyber offence. The remedy here lies with consumer forums, not cybercrime law.
punishment: Not applicable as a cybercrime - this is a consumer protection/civil matter, remediable through consumer courts or the platform's grievance redressal.

situation: An online seller refused to issue a refund for a defective product, citing their 'no refund' policy, which I find unfair but was clearly stated at checkout.
explanation: A dispute over a seller's stated refund policy, when the policy was disclosed in advance, is a consumer rights/contractual matter rather than a criminal offence, unless the product was deliberately misrepresented to defraud the buyer. This falls under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, including its E-Commerce Rules.
punishment: Not applicable as a cybercrime - civil/consumer protection matter.

situation: A hacking group claimed responsibility for breaching India's power grid control systems and threatened to cause blackouts unless their political demands are met.
ipc_sections: Read with Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, as applicable
bns_sections: Read with Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, as applicable
explanation: This is among the gravest offences under Indian cyber law. Section 66F criminalizes acts that deny or disrupt access to critical information infrastructure, or attempt to penetrate/access a computer resource without authorization, with intent to threaten the unity, integrity, security, or sovereignty of India, or to strike terror in people. Attacking power grid control systems for coercive political demands fits this provision precisely and would likely also invoke the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967.
punishment: Section 66F: imprisonment for life.

situation: An employee downloaded our company's entire client database and source code onto a personal USB drive before resigning and joining a competitor.
it_act_sections: Section 72 (breach of confidentiality, if intermediary obligations apply)
ipc_sections: Section 408 (criminal breach of trust by employee)
bns_sections: Section 316(3) BNS (criminal breach of trust by employee)
explanation: Unauthorized extraction and removal of confidential business data (client databases, proprietary source code) by an employee, especially for use at a competing organization, constitutes both theft of data under IT Act Sections 43/66 and criminal breach of trust by an employee under BNS Section 316(3), which carries enhanced punishment due to the position of trust.
punishment: Section 66: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh. Criminal breach of trust by employee under BNS 316(3): up to 10 years imprisonment and fine, reflecting the breach of a position of trust.

situation: I left my previous job and took my own personal notes and learnings (not company-owned data) with me to use as general knowledge in my new role.
explanation: An individual's own general knowledge, skills, and personal learning acquired during employment are not the property of the employer and can be lawfully carried forward, as long as no confidential company data, trade secrets, or proprietary materials are involved. This is a settled principle distinguishing general skill from confidential information.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out, since no proprietary company data was taken.

situation: I received a message on Instagram from an account claiming to be a modeling agency, offering me a contract, but then asking me to pay a 'registration fee' upfront via UPI.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: This is a common advance-fee scam where a fake opportunity is dangled to dishonestly induce upfront payment. If payment has been made, this constitutes completed cheating via a computer resource under Section 66D of the IT Act and BNS Section 318.
punishment: Section 66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh. BNS 318: up to 7 years depending on severity and clause.

situation: Someone on a job portal asked me to pay a 'security deposit' before I could be considered for a work-from-home data entry job, and after I paid, they stopped responding.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: This is a fake job scam, a recognized pattern of online fraud where fraudulent job postings are used to extract upfront payments under false pretenses via electronic platforms, attracting Section 66D of the IT Act for cheating by personation through a computer resource.
punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh under Section 66D; BNS 318 cheating provisions may extend this further depending on amount and intent shown.

situation: I applied for a genuine work-from-home job through a verified company's official careers page and went through a normal multi-round interview process.
explanation: Applying for and going through a legitimate hiring process with a verified employer through official channels is a normal, lawful activity with no element of deception or unauthorized access involved.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: I forgot my own email password and used the 'forgot password' option to reset it using my registered phone number.
explanation: Using the legitimate, intended account-recovery mechanism to regain access to one's own account is normal authorized use, not unauthorized access. There is no cyber offence here.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: My phone suddenly lost network signal, and within hours I discovered my bank account had been emptied; later I learned someone had fraudulently obtained a duplicate SIM card in my number.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: This is a SIM swap fraud, where the fraudster impersonates the victim to the telecom provider to obtain a duplicate SIM, then uses OTP-based access to drain the victim's bank account. This involves identity theft (Section 66C) and cheating by personation through a computer/telecom resource (Section 66D), and is also reportable to the Department of Telecommunications.
punishment: Section 66C/66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh each. Cheating under BNS 318 can extend up to 7 years depending on amount involved.

situation: I switched my mobile number from one telecom operator to another using the official MNP (mobile number portability) process, which took a couple of days as expected.
explanation: Mobile Number Portability is a legitimate, regulated process offered by telecom operators with the subscriber's own consent and verification (typically via UPC code sent to the user). This is routine and lawful telecom activity.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: Someone used AI tools to create a deepfake video of me saying things I never said and circulated it among my professional network, damaging my credibility.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: Creating and circulating a deepfake that falsely attributes statements to a real person is a form of personation and identity misuse under Section 66D, combined with privacy violation under Section 66E, and defamation under BNS Section 356 since it damages reputation through false attribution. India does not yet have a dedicated deepfake-specific statute, so prosecution currently relies on this combination of provisions; the IT Rules 2021 (as amended) also impose takedown obligations on platforms for synthetic/manipulated media.
punishment: Section 66D/66E: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1-2 lakh. Defamation under BNS 356: up to 2 years imprisonment, or fine, or both.

situation: A deepfake video using a female celebrity's face was superimposed onto explicit content and circulated widely on social media without her consent.
it_act_sections: Section 67A (sexually explicit material in electronic form)
explanation: Non-consensual sexually explicit deepfakes constitute a severe privacy violation under Section 66E and squarely fall under Section 67A of the IT Act for publishing/transmitting sexually explicit material electronically, since the underlying act causes the same harm to the depicted individual regardless of whether the imagery is real or synthetically generated.
punishment: Section 67A: up to 5 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 10 lakh for first conviction; up to 7 years and fine up to Rs. 10 lakh for subsequent conviction.

situation: I used an AI image generator to create a fictional, clearly-labeled satirical cartoon of a public policy debate for my blog, not depicting any real identifiable person.
explanation: Creating clearly fictional, non-defamatory satirical content that does not depict or impersonate any real identifiable individual is a lawful exercise of creative and political expression, protected under free speech principles.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: I deposited money into an online betting app that promised guaranteed winnings on cricket matches, but when I tried to withdraw my winnings, the app blocked my account and stopped responding.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: Fraudulent gaming/betting platforms that accept deposits but block withdrawals constitute cheating committed via a computer resource under Section 66D of the IT Act. Note that online betting itself may also raise issues under state-specific gambling laws, separate from the fraud committed by the platform.
punishment: Section 66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh. BNS 318 (cheating): up to 7 years depending on severity.

situation: My nephew spent money on in-game purchases (skins and upgrades) in a mobile game using my saved card without my knowledge, since the card was saved on my phone with the app.
it_act_sections: Section 66C (if card/identity details were used without authorization) - civil/family context tempers criminal pursuit
explanation: Technically, using saved payment details without the cardholder's authorization could fall under unauthorized use of payment credentials. However, where the person making the unauthorized purchases is a minor family member without fraudulent intent (rather than an external attacker), this is typically resolved as a family/consumer matter through the app's refund policies and parental control settings rather than criminal prosecution, since the legal threshold for criminal intent (mens rea) is unlikely to be met.
punishment: Generally resolved via the platform's refund/dispute process rather than criminal prosecution in family contexts; formal criminal liability would require deceptive intent, which is typically absent here.

situation: I play a multiplayer online game with friends regularly and sometimes spend money on legitimate in-app purchases using my own card.
explanation: Voluntary spending on legitimate in-game purchases using one's own payment method is a normal consumer transaction with no element of fraud, deception, or unauthorized access.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: I met someone on a matrimonial website, and after weeks of conversation, they claimed to be stuck abroad and needed money urgently for a medical emergency, after which they stopped responding once I sent the funds.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: This is a classic romance scam, where a fraudster builds trust over time through a matrimonial or dating platform before fabricating an emergency to extract money. The deception conducted via a computer resource (the platform/messaging) constitutes cheating by personation under Section 66D, alongside cheating under BNS Section 318.
punishment: Section 66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh. BNS 318 (cheating): up to 7 years depending on the amount and clause invoked.

situation: My family is using a matrimonial website to find a suitable match for me, and we've been verifying profiles before proceeding to meet anyone.
explanation: Using a legitimate matrimonial platform with reasonable verification before proceeding is a normal, lawful, and prudent way to seek a match. No deception or fraud is involved.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: Someone posted my home address, phone number, and daily schedule on a public forum after I criticized them online, encouraging others to 'visit' me.
it_act_sections: Section 43 (if data was obtained through unauthorized access)
explanation: This is doxxing - publishing someone's private identifying information online with intent to enable harassment or harm. This violates Section 66E (privacy violation) and, given the implicit threat of having strangers 'visit,' constitutes criminal intimidation under BNS Section 351. If the conduct is part of an ongoing pattern, cyberstalking provisions may also apply.
punishment: Section 66E: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 2 lakh. Criminal intimidation under BNS 351: up to 2 years or fine or both (up to 7 years for threats of death/grievous hurt).

situation: A journalist published a news article naming a public official and their officially listed work address and office phone number in connection with a government policy story.
explanation: Publishing publicly available, official contact information of a public official in their professional capacity, in connection with legitimate journalism on a matter of public interest, is standard journalistic practice and not a privacy violation, since this is information the official has provided for public/professional accessibility.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out, as this involves public-facing professional information used for legitimate journalism.

situation: A rival company hired a hacker to break into our internal servers and steal our unreleased product designs before our official launch.
ipc_sections: Section 420 (cheating, if used to gain unfair business advantage)
explanation: Corporate espionage involving unauthorized intrusion into a competitor's systems to steal trade secrets or proprietary designs is a serious offence under Section 66 of the IT Act (computer related offences flowing from Section 43's prohibition on unauthorized access). The company that commissioned the hack can also be held liable for abetment.
punishment: Section 66: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh for the hacker; abetment carries similar liability for those who commissioned the act under general criminal law principles.

situation: Our marketing team studied a competitor's publicly available pricing page and social media posts to benchmark our own product pricing strategy.
explanation: Competitive analysis using publicly available information is standard, lawful business practice and a normal part of market research. No unauthorized access or data theft is involved.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: Someone hacked into the university's exam portal and changed their grades from failing to passing across multiple subjects.
it_act_sections: Section 43 (unauthorized access and alteration of data)
explanation: Unauthorized access to an academic records system to fraudulently alter grade data is a clear violation of Section 43 (unauthorized access and data alteration), criminally punishable under Section 66, combined with forgery of academic records under the BNS, since the falsified records are intended to be used as genuine.
punishment: Section 66: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh. Forgery under BNS 336 can attract up to 7 years depending on the nature of the document forged.

situation: I checked my exam results on the university's official student portal using my own login credentials after results were declared.
explanation: Logging into one's own account through official, authorized means to check one's own results is normal, authorized use of a system.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: An employee who had legitimate access to company financial records as part of their job discovered evidence of fraud and shared the relevant documents with a government regulator.
explanation: Disclosure of evidence of wrongdoing to appropriate regulatory or law enforcement authorities by someone who had legitimate access to the information, made in good faith and in the public interest, is generally protected whistleblowing activity rather than a cyber offence. India's Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 and various sectoral regulations provide some protections in such cases, though the scope of protection can vary by context and employer type.
punishment: Not applicable as a cybercrime - this is a whistleblowing/regulatory disclosure matter, though specific facts should be reviewed against applicable confidentiality agreements and protection statutes.

situation: A disgruntled employee downloaded confidential customer data they were not authorized to access and leaked it to a journalist to embarrass the company, unrelated to any wrongdoing by the company.
explanation: Unlike genuine whistleblowing about wrongdoing, accessing data beyond one's authorization and leaking it for personal grievance rather than to expose illegality is unauthorized access and a breach of trust under Sections 43 and 66 of the IT Act, combined with criminal breach of trust under the BNS, since there is no protected public-interest disclosure involved.
punishment: Section 66: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh. Criminal breach of trust under BNS 316: up to 5-10 years depending on the specific clause.

situation: My 14-year-old child was added to an online group chat by classmates where older, unknown adults were also present, and one adult began asking my child for personal photos.
it_act_sections: Section 67B (if sexual content/solicitation of children is involved)
explanation: An adult soliciting personal photos from a minor online, especially in the context of online grooming, raises serious child safety concerns. Depending on the nature of the photos requested and any subsequent acts, this can fall under Section 67B of the IT Act, and the POCSO Act, 2012, which specifically criminalizes online sexual solicitation and grooming of children (Section 11/12 read with related provisions). This should be reported immediately to the Cyber Crime helpline (1930) or cybercrime.gov.in, and to local police/child protection authorities.
punishment: Section 67B: up to 5-7 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 10 lakh. POCSO penalties for grooming/solicitation can be additionally severe and run concurrently.

situation: My child uses an educational app at school that requires a teacher-supervised login and only accesses age-appropriate, curriculum-approved content.
explanation: Use of a supervised, age-appropriate educational platform within an institutional setting with appropriate safeguards is normal and beneficial use of technology, posing no cyber safety concern.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: Someone gained access to my cryptocurrency wallet through a fake wallet-recovery website and transferred all my Bitcoin holdings to an unknown address.
explanation: Using a fraudulent phishing website to obtain wallet recovery phrases/private keys and then transferring cryptocurrency without authorization is a combination of unauthorized access (Section 43/66), identity theft of wallet credentials (Section 66C), and cheating by personation (Section 66D). Cryptocurrency, while not legal tender in India, is treated as property for the purposes of theft and fraud prosecution.
punishment: Section 66: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh. Section 66C/66D: up to 3 years and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh each.

situation: I bought Bitcoin through a registered, RBI-compliant Indian cryptocurrency exchange using my own bank account and properly completed KYC.
explanation: Purchasing cryptocurrency through a legitimate, KYC-compliant exchange following applicable regulatory requirements is a lawful financial transaction.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: A company is selling cracked/pirated versions of expensive enterprise software licenses through a website, bypassing the original vendor's licensing checks.
it_act_sections: Section 65 (tampering with computer source documents, if source code/licensing mechanism was altered)
explanation: Distributing cracked software that circumvents licensing/DRM mechanisms involves tampering with computer source code under Section 65 of the IT Act (if the source documents were altered) and is primarily prosecuted under the Copyright Act, 1957, which criminalizes circumvention of technological protection measures and infringement of copyright in software.
punishment: Section 65 IT Act: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 2 lakh. Copyright Act offences: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 2 lakh, which can run concurrently.

situation: I use a free, open-source software tool under its published license terms for a personal coding project.
explanation: Using open-source software in accordance with its published license terms is fully lawful and is precisely the intended use case for such licenses.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: I received an email claiming to be from the Income Tax Department saying I have a pending refund and asking me to click a link and enter my bank details to claim it.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation of a government entity using computer resource)
explanation: This is a phishing scam impersonating a government department to extract sensitive financial information. Falsely posing as a government authority through electronic communication to deceive a person constitutes cheating by personation under Section 66D of the IT Act, an aggravated form of the offence given the impersonation of a state authority.
punishment: Section 66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh. Impersonating a government servant can additionally attract penalties under general criminal law provisions for impersonation of public servants.

situation: I received a genuine SMS from my state government's official short code confirming my passport application status update.
explanation: Receiving legitimate official communication from a verified government short code regarding one's own application is normal, authentic government service delivery.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: My former partner shared intimate photos and videos of us, taken consensually during our relationship, on a public website after we broke up, without my consent.
explanation: This is non-consensual intimate imagery ('revenge porn'). Even though the images were originally taken consensually, publishing or transmitting them without the subject's consent after the relationship ended is a serious violation of privacy under Section 66E and squarely falls under Section 67A of the IT Act for transmitting sexually explicit material electronically without consent. Courts and cybercrime cells in India treat this as a high-priority offence, and victims can seek urgent takedown under the IT Rules 2021 in addition to criminal prosecution.
punishment: Section 67A: up to 5 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 10 lakh for first conviction; up to 7 years and fine up to Rs. 10 lakh for subsequent conviction. Section 66E: up to 3 years and/or fine up to Rs. 2 lakh.

situation: Two business partners are in a dispute over who owns a jointly registered company domain name and social media accounts, and one has refused to hand over login access.
explanation: Disputes over ownership of jointly-created digital business assets between partners, where both had legitimate original access, are primarily civil/contractual and partnership law matters, not criminal cyber offences, unless one party obtains access through deception or hacks an account they were never authorized to access in the first place. This is typically resolved through partnership dissolution agreements or civil suits.
punishment: Not applicable as a cybercrime in the absence of unauthorized access or deception - this is a civil/partnership dispute, resolvable through negotiation, mediation, or civil courts.

situation: A subscription service automatically renewed and charged my card because I forgot to cancel before the trial period ended, even though the terms clearly disclosed this at signup.
explanation: Auto-renewal charges that were clearly disclosed in the terms at the time of signup, even if the consumer forgot to cancel, do not constitute fraud, since there was no deception about the billing terms. This is a consumer awareness matter, though under Indian consumer protection rules companies are required to send renewal reminders; if such reminders were not sent as legally mandated, it could become a consumer protection complaint rather than a cybercrime.
punishment: Not applicable as a cybercrime - consumer protection matter, addressable through the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, or the service's own cancellation/refund process.

situation: I'm a security researcher who found a vulnerability in a company's public website and reported it responsibly to them through their official bug bounty program without exploiting it further.
explanation: Responsible disclosure of security vulnerabilities through an authorized bug bounty or responsible disclosure program, without unauthorized exploitation, data theft, or damage, is a recognized and legally protected cybersecurity practice. Most organizations explicitly authorize this kind of testing within defined scope, which negates the 'unauthorized access' element required for liability under Section 43/66.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out when conducted within the authorized scope of a responsible disclosure or bug bounty program.

situation: A security researcher found a vulnerability in a bank's mobile app and, instead of reporting it, used it to access other customers' account information to prove a point on social media.
explanation: Even when initially motivated by security research, actually exploiting a vulnerability to access other customers' confidential account data without authorization, rather than responsibly disclosing it, crosses into unauthorized access and a breach of confidentiality, both punishable under Sections 43, 66, and 72 of the IT Act. Good intent does not exempt unauthorized access to others' private data.
punishment: Section 66: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh. Section 72: up to 2 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 1 lakh.

situation: My employer monitors company-issued laptops and email accounts for security and compliance purposes, as disclosed in our employment contract and IT policy.
explanation: Employer monitoring of company-owned devices and accounts, when clearly disclosed in advance through employment contracts or IT policies, is a standard and lawful corporate governance practice, not a privacy violation, since the employee has been informed and the monitoring relates to company property and resources.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out, as monitoring was disclosed and relates to company-owned resources.

situation: Someone created a parody account clearly labeled as 'parody/fan account, not affiliated' that humorously mimics a celebrity's public persona and posts obviously satirical content.
explanation: Clearly labeled parody or fan accounts that do not attempt to deceive followers into believing they are the genuine, official account are generally protected as satire and free expression, since they lack the deceptive intent that distinguishes parody from impersonation under Sections 66C/66D.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out when the account is clearly and genuinely labeled as parody/fan content without deceptive intent.

situation: A scammer created a fake account pretending to be a celebrity (without any parody disclosure) and used it to solicit money from fans for a 'fan meet-and-greet contest' that never existed.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: Unlike disclosed parody, this involves deliberately impersonating a real individual without disclosure, specifically to deceive victims into parting with money, which is a clear case of identity theft (Section 66C) combined with cheating by personation through a computer resource (Section 66D).
punishment: Section 66C/66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh each. BNS cheating provisions can extend this further depending on the amount defrauded.

situation: I sent a strongly worded but non-threatening email to a company's customer service complaining about poor service and demanding a refund.
explanation: Expressing dissatisfaction and demanding a legitimate remedy through a company's official customer service channel, without threats or abuse, is a normal exercise of consumer rights.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: An anonymous account has been sending me messages threatening to harm me and my family if I don't pay them a sum of money in cryptocurrency, claiming to have compromising information about me.
explanation: This is cyber extortion - using threats made through electronic communication to coerce payment. This is criminal intimidation and extortion under BNS Sections 351 and 308, and if the 'compromising information' includes private images, Section 66E of the IT Act also applies for the underlying privacy violation.
punishment: Extortion under BNS 308: up to 7 years imprisonment along with fine. Criminal intimidation under BNS 351: up to 2 years or fine or both (up to 7 years if death/grievous hurt is threatened).

situation: I run a small online business and use Google Analytics to track anonymized visitor traffic and behavior patterns on my own website.
explanation: Using standard, industry-common analytics tools to track aggregated and/or anonymized visitor behavior on one's own legitimately owned website is normal business practice, especially when done in compliance with applicable privacy disclosures (e.g., cookie consent banners).
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out, provided appropriate privacy disclosures/consent mechanisms are in place as required by applicable law.

situation: Someone hijacked my YouTube channel by tricking me into clicking a fake brand-collaboration link that stole my login session, and they are now live-streaming a cryptocurrency scam using my channel's subscriber base.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation, re: scam content)
bns_sections: Section 318 BNS (cheating, for the downstream scam)
explanation: This combines account hijacking via a phishing link (unauthorized access under Sections 43/66) with the subsequent use of the compromised channel to run a cheating scheme that defrauds viewers (Section 66D and BNS 318). This is a well-documented attack pattern targeting content creators.
punishment: Section 66: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh. Section 66D: up to 3 years and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh. Downstream cheating victims can pursue separate complaints under BNS 318.

situation: My landlord installed a hidden camera in the bathroom of the rental property I'm living in, and I discovered it was streaming footage to an app on his phone.
it_act_sections: Section 66E (violation of privacy, capturing/transmitting images of private area without consent)
explanation: Covertly capturing and transmitting images of a person in a private space where they have a reasonable expectation of privacy (such as a bathroom), without their consent, is a serious privacy violation under Section 66E of the IT Act and constitutes voyeurism under BNS Section 77.
punishment: Section 66E: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 2 lakh. Voyeurism under BNS 77: up to 3 years for first conviction (up to 7 years for subsequent conviction), along with fine.

situation: A retail store has visible CCTV cameras in the customer area for security purposes, clearly displayed with signage indicating recording is in progress.
explanation: Visible, disclosed CCTV surveillance in common/public commercial areas for legitimate security purposes is standard, lawful practice and does not violate any reasonable expectation of privacy, especially when disclosed via signage.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: I received a WhatsApp message from an unknown number offering me a part-time job of 'liking YouTube videos' for daily payment, and after completing a few small tasks and getting paid, they asked me to join a 'VIP group' requiring an upfront investment.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: This is a well-known 'task-based investment scam' pattern, where small initial payments build trust before victims are persuaded to make larger 'investments' that are never returned. The entire scheme operated through electronic messaging to defraud constitutes cheating via computer resource under Section 66D of the IT Act.
punishment: Section 66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh. BNS 318 cheating provisions can extend punishment up to 7 years depending on amount and scale.

situation: I use two-factor authentication and a password manager to secure my online accounts, and I recently updated all my passwords as a precaution after a major data breach was reported in the news.
explanation: Taking proactive cybersecurity precautions to protect one's own accounts is responsible, lawful digital hygiene, not a cyber offence.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: A disgruntled customer posted hundreds of fake negative reviews using multiple fake accounts to deliberately tank a small business's rating after a personal dispute with the owner unrelated to the product or service quality.
it_act_sections: Section 66C (identity theft, if fake accounts impersonate real people)
Section 66D (if fake personas are used to deceive)
explanation: Posting numerous fake reviews through multiple fabricated accounts, motivated by personal malice rather than genuine experience, to defame and harm a business constitutes defamation under BNS Section 356. If the fake accounts impersonate real third parties without consent, identity theft under Section 66C also applies.
punishment: Defamation under BNS 356: up to 2 years imprisonment, or fine, or both, or community service. Section 66C (if applicable): up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh.

situation: I'm comparing two products on my YouTube tech review channel and pointing out genuine flaws I personally found during testing of both.
explanation: Honest, fact-based product reviews and comparisons based on genuine personal testing are legitimate consumer journalism/commentary and are protected as fair comment, provided the criticism is truthful and not maliciously fabricated.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: An online tutoring platform I used shared my child's learning progress data with a third-party advertising company without proper parental consent, as later revealed through a privacy investigation.
it_act_sections: Section 43A (failure to protect sensitive personal data)
Section 72A (disclosure of information in breach of lawful contract)
explanation: Sharing a child's personal data with third parties without proper parental consent is a serious violation under Section 43A (failure to implement reasonable security/privacy practices) and Section 72A of the IT Act (unauthorized disclosure of personal information obtained under a service contract). This would also likely violate the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, which has heightened consent requirements for processing children's data.
punishment: Section 43A: compensation as determined by adjudicating authority, uncapped. Section 72A: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh for the responsible individual. DPDP Act penalties on the company can run into crores of rupees.

situation: A telemarketer called me to offer a credit card, and I declined and asked to be removed from their calling list, which they complied with.
explanation: A standard, compliant telemarketing call that respects an opt-out request is a normal commercial practice, particularly when handled in line with TRAI's regulations on commercial communications.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: A developer at our company secretly modified the source code of our flagship product to insert a hidden backdoor before quitting, allowing him remote access even after leaving.
ipc_sections: Section 408 (criminal breach of trust by employee)
bns_sections: Section 316(3) BNS (criminal breach of trust by employee)
explanation: Knowingly or intentionally concealing, destroying, or altering computer source code when it is required to be kept or maintained, with the intent to cause damage, is specifically criminalized under Section 65 of the IT Act. Embedding a hidden backdoor for unauthorized future access compounds this with Sections 43 and 66, plus criminal breach of trust by an employee under the BNS given the position of trust.
punishment: Section 65: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 2 lakh. Section 66: up to 3 years and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh. Criminal breach of trust by employee under BNS 316(3): up to 10 years imprisonment.

situation: Our development team uses version control (Git) to track and review all changes to our codebase, with mandatory code review before any change is merged.
explanation: Standard, authorized software development practices like version control and peer code review represent normal, lawful engineering workflow with full transparency and accountability for changes made.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: A competitor allegedly launched a coordinated DDoS (distributed denial of service) attack against our e-commerce website during our biggest sale event, causing it to crash for six hours and resulting in significant revenue loss.
it_act_sections: Section 43 (denial of access to authorized users)
Section 66F (cyber terrorism, only if critical infrastructure/national security angle exists - not typical for commercial DDoS)
explanation: A Distributed Denial of Service attack that deliberately disrupts access to a computer resource for authorized users is explicitly covered under Section 43(f) of the IT Act (denying access to an authorized person), criminally punishable under Section 66, combined with mischief provisions under the BNS for the resulting financial damage.
punishment: Section 66: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh. Mischief causing damage under BNS 324 can attract penalties scaled to the value of loss caused.

situation: Our website experienced a temporary slowdown during a flash sale simply due to unexpectedly high genuine customer traffic, not any malicious attack.
explanation: A service slowdown caused by legitimate high traffic volume, without any malicious intent or unauthorized interference, is purely an infrastructure/capacity issue, not a cyber offence.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: I downloaded a flashlight app from a third-party app store that, after installation, started sending premium-rate SMS messages from my phone without my knowledge, resulting in unexpected charges on my phone bill.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: A malicious app that performs unauthorized actions (sending premium SMS) without the user's knowledge or consent constitutes introduction of a computer contaminant and unauthorized use of the device under Sections 43 and 66 of the IT Act, combined with cheating under Section 66D/BNS 318 since the user is fraudulently charged.
punishment: Section 66: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh. Section 66D: up to 3 years and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh.

situation: I downloaded a well-reviewed fitness tracking app from the official Google Play Store and granted it permission to access my step count data, as disclosed in its privacy policy.
explanation: Downloading a legitimate app from an official app store and granting permissions that are clearly disclosed and relevant to the app's stated function is normal, informed, consensual use of technology.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: I received a panicked phone call that sounded exactly like my son's voice saying he'd been in an accident and needed money sent immediately, but it turned out to be an AI-generated voice clone scam.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: This is an AI voice-cloning scam, an increasingly common fraud where attackers use a brief audio sample (often scraped from social media) to clone a victim's voice and stage a fake emergency. Impersonating a real person's voice to deceive a third party into transferring money is identity theft (Section 66C) combined with cheating by personation through a computer/telecom resource (Section 66D).
punishment: Section 66C/66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh each. BNS cheating provisions under Section 318 can extend punishment up to 7 years depending on amount involved.

situation: I won an online auction for a vintage watch and paid the seller via bank transfer as instructed, but the seller never shipped the item and disappeared from the platform.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: A seller who collects payment through an online platform without any genuine intention to deliver the purchased item has committed cheating via a computer resource under Section 66D of the IT Act, combined with cheating under BNS Section 318.
punishment: Section 66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh. BNS 318: up to 7 years depending on the clause and value involved.

situation: I bought a used car through a classifieds website after personally inspecting it, test-driving it, and verifying the registration documents before paying.
explanation: A transaction where the buyer conducted reasonable due diligence (inspection, test drive, document verification) before a voluntary purchase is a normal, legitimate commercial transaction, regardless of the platform used to find the listing.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: Someone took control of my business's official Instagram account with 500,000 followers and is demanding Rs. 2 lakh in exchange for returning access, threatening to delete the account otherwise.
explanation: This combines unauthorized access/account hijacking under Sections 43 and 66 of the IT Act with extortion under BNS Section 308, since the attacker is using unauthorized control as leverage to coerce a ransom payment.
punishment: Section 66: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh. Extortion under BNS 308: up to 7 years imprisonment along with fine.

situation: A coordinated network of fake social media accounts is spreading fabricated polling data and fake statements attributed to election candidates just before voting day, designed to look like genuine news.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation, re: fake accounts impersonating real entities)
IT Rules 2021 (synthetic/misleading content obligations on platforms)
ipc_sections: Section 171G (false statements in connection with election, where applicable)
bns_sections: Section 353 BNS (statements conducing to public mischief)
explanation: Coordinated fake accounts spreading fabricated information designed to influence an election, especially when impersonating real candidates or fabricating attributed statements, can attract Section 66D (personation), public mischief provisions under BNS Section 353, and election-specific offences under the Representation of the People Act, 1951, in addition to platform-level takedown obligations under the IT Rules, 2021.
punishment: BNS Section 353: imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine, or both. Election law offences carry separate penalties under the Representation of the People Act, 1951, including potential disqualification for candidates found responsible.

situation: I shared a news article about an upcoming election from a credible, verified mainstream news outlet on my personal social media account with my own honest commentary.
explanation: Sharing factual news from a credible, verified source along with one's own genuine commentary is a normal exercise of free expression and civic engagement, not misinformation.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: I keep receiving hundreds of unsolicited promotional SMS messages daily from various companies despite never having given consent and having registered on the DND (Do Not Disturb) list.
it_act_sections: IT Act does not directly criminalize spam; primarily governed by TRAI regulations
explanation: Unsolicited commercial communication sent despite DND registration is primarily regulated under the Telecom Commercial Communications Customer Preference Regulations (TCCCPR) enforced by TRAI, rather than the IT Act, IPC, or BNS. While not a 'cybercrime' in the traditional sense, repeated violations can result in regulatory penalties against the sender and can be reported through the TRAI DND app or to the telecom operator.
punishment: Regulatory penalties under TRAI regulations for senders/telemarketers found in violation, rather than criminal imprisonment; complaints can be filed via the 'DND' app or by sending an SMS to 1909.

situation: A company I'm a registered customer of sends me occasional promotional emails about new products, with a clear and functional unsubscribe link in every email.
explanation: Promotional communication sent to existing customers with proper opt-out mechanisms in compliance with applicable regulations is standard, lawful marketing practice.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: A buyer on an online marketplace asked me to share an OTP to 'verify the transaction' before paying for the item I was selling, and after I shared it, I realized money was deducted from my own account instead of being credited.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: This is a 'reverse OTP' or 'collect request' scam targeting sellers on online marketplaces, where the fraudster disguises a payment-collection request as a payment-receipt verification. The deception is carried out through a computer resource, attracting Section 66D of the IT Act, combined with Section 66C for OTP/credential misuse.
punishment: Section 66C/66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh each. BNS 318 (cheating): up to 7 years depending on the amount and clause invoked.

situation: I shared an OTP with my bank's official customer care representative after I called the bank's verified number myself to resolve a card issue, as part of their standard identity verification process.
explanation: Sharing an OTP with a verified bank representative through a call initiated by the customer themselves to the bank's official number, as part of standard identity verification, is normal and safe banking practice, distinct from sharing an OTP with an unsolicited caller.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: A hacktivist group defaced our organization's official website, replacing the homepage with political slogans and propaganda images, without authorization.
it_act_sections: Section 43 (unauthorized access and alteration of data)
Section 70 (if the website is a 'protected system' under government notification)
explanation: Unauthorized access to alter or deface a website constitutes a clear violation of Section 43 (unauthorized access and data alteration), punishable under Section 66 of the IT Act. If the targeted website belongs to a critical government or protected system formally notified under Section 70, much more severe penalties under that section apply instead.
punishment: Section 66: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh. Section 70 (protected systems): up to 10 years imprisonment and fine, if applicable.
