situation: Someone submitted a fraudulent online insurance claim using my policy number and personal details, which I never authorized, to claim a payout for a fake incident.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: Using another person's policy details and identity to fraudulently file an insurance claim through an online portal is identity theft under Section 66C, combined with cheating by personation through a computer resource under Section 66D.
punishment: Section 66C/66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh each. BNS cheating provisions can extend punishment further based on claim value.

situation: I filed a genuine insurance claim online for a car accident, submitting accurate photos, the police FIR copy, and repair estimates as required by my insurer.
explanation: Filing a truthful, well-documented insurance claim for an actual covered event through the insurer's official online process is normal, lawful policyholder activity.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: A client on a freelancing platform received my completed project deliverables but then disputed the payment with the platform, falsely claiming the work was never delivered, even though I have timestamped proof of delivery.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (if false claims involve fabricated electronic evidence to deceive the platform)
explanation: If a client knowingly makes a false claim to defraud a freelancer of legitimately earned payment, and especially if they fabricate or falsify evidence submitted to the platform's dispute system, this constitutes cheating via a computer resource under Section 66D. However, in many cases such disputes are resolved by the platform's own evidence-based resolution process without rising to a formal criminal complaint, and falls more naturally into a civil/contractual dispute unless clear fraudulent intent and fabrication are demonstrated.
punishment: If fraudulent intent is established: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh under Section 66D. Many such disputes are otherwise resolved through the freelancing platform's grievance/arbitration mechanism.

situation: A client and I had a genuine disagreement about whether the final freelance deliverable met the originally agreed scope, and we're working through the platform's standard revision process.
explanation: A genuine, good-faith disagreement about deliverable scope or quality, being resolved through the platform's normal revision and dispute process, is an ordinary contractual matter, not a cyber offence.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: A website is selling counterfeit prescription medications online, falsely claiming they are genuine, without requiring any valid prescription.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation, re: fake legitimacy claims)
ipc_sections: Read with Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940
bns_sections: Read with Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940
explanation: Selling counterfeit medications online while falsely representing them as genuine constitutes cheating committed via a computer resource under Section 66D, in addition to serious violations under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, which separately and severely penalizes the sale of spurious/counterfeit drugs given the public health risk involved.
punishment: Section 66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh. Drugs and Cosmetics Act offences for spurious drugs can carry penalties up to life imprisonment depending on the harm caused.

situation: I ordered genuine over-the-counter medication from a licensed online pharmacy that verified my prescription as required for prescription-only items.
explanation: Purchasing genuine medication from a licensed, compliant online pharmacy that follows proper prescription verification protocols is a lawful healthcare transaction.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: My spouse and I share access to each other's phones and social media accounts by mutual agreement as part of our relationship, and occasionally check each other's messages with consent.
explanation: Mutually consensual sharing of access between adults in a relationship, where both parties have knowingly and voluntarily agreed to the arrangement, does not constitute unauthorized access, since consent negates the core element required for an offence under Section 43/66 of the IT Act.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out, given mutual, ongoing, voluntary consent.

situation: My spouse secretly installed spyware on my phone to monitor my messages and location without my knowledge, after I had explicitly refused to share that access.
explanation: Even within a marriage, installing spyware to covertly monitor a spouse's private communications and location without their knowledge or consent, especially after they have explicitly refused such access, constitutes unauthorized access under Sections 43 and 66 and a privacy violation under Section 66E of the IT Act. Marital status does not provide blanket legal immunity for unauthorized surveillance.
punishment: Section 66: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh. Section 66E: up to 3 years and/or fine up to Rs. 2 lakh.

situation: Parents installed a parental control app on their 10-year-old child's tablet to monitor screen time and block inappropriate content, which the child is aware of.
explanation: Parental monitoring of a minor child's device for legitimate safety and developmental supervision purposes is a normal and legally recognized exercise of parental responsibility, especially for young children.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: A company sent me a legitimate password reset confirmation email after I clicked 'forgot password' on their login page myself.
explanation: A password reset confirmation triggered by the account holder's own request through the legitimate recovery flow is standard, expected account security functionality.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: I received a legal notice via email from a law firm regarding a genuine contractual dispute with a former business associate, which appears to be authentic and properly addressed to me.
explanation: Receiving a legitimate legal notice through email regarding an actual dispute is a normal part of legal process and dispute resolution, not a cyber offence.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out, though the underlying contractual dispute itself may warrant separate legal consultation.

situation: Someone is selling stolen credit card data ('dumps') on a dark web marketplace, including card numbers and CVVs scraped from a previous data breach.
ipc_sections: Section 411 (dishonestly receiving stolen property, as applied to data)
explanation: Trading in stolen financial credentials is a severe combination of identity theft (Section 66C) and computer-related offences (Section 66) under the IT Act, since the data itself was unlawfully obtained and its further sale/distribution perpetuates the fraud against the original cardholders. This is actively monitored by India's Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C).
punishment: Section 66C: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh. Section 66: up to 3 years and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh. Receiving stolen property under BNS 317 can attract up to 3 years imprisonment.

situation: A bank's fraud detection system flagged and blocked a genuine large transaction I made, requiring me to call customer care to verify and unblock it.
explanation: Standard fraud-prevention measures by a bank that temporarily flag unusual but legitimate transactions for verification are normal security practices designed to protect customers, not a cyber offence.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: An anonymous Twitter/X account has been posting a coordinated series of threatening messages targeting a specific journalist for her reporting, including threats of sexual violence, over several weeks.
it_act_sections: Section 67 (publishing obscene/sexually threatening content electronically, if applicable)
Section 66E (if private images are also threatened/shared)
ipc_sections: Section 506 (criminal intimidation, including for threats of sexual violence which carries enhanced punishment)
explanation: A sustained, coordinated campaign of threats, particularly involving threats of sexual violence against a journalist for their professional work, constitutes serious cyberstalking under BNS Section 78 and criminal intimidation under Section 351, which carries enhanced punishment specifically for threats involving rape or grievous harm.
punishment: Stalking under BNS 78: up to 3-5 years imprisonment with fine. Criminal intimidation involving threats of death/grievous hurt/sexual violence under BNS 351: up to 7 years imprisonment, or fine, or both.

situation: I post my opinions about movies and books on a public book-review blog using my real name, and sometimes people disagree with me in the comments respectfully.
explanation: Sharing personal opinions publicly and engaging in respectful disagreement in comments is normal, healthy public discourse, not a cyber offence.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: A fraudulent caller posing as a 'TRAI official' told me my mobile number would be disconnected in 2 hours due to 'illegal activity' unless I pressed 9 to connect to a fake 'cybercrime officer,' who then asked for my banking app screen-share access.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: This is the 'digital arrest'/fake regulator scam pattern that has become widespread in India, where fraudsters impersonate telecom regulators, police, or cybercrime officials to intimidate victims into granting remote access or transferring funds. This involves cheating by personation of an official authority under Section 66D, and if remote screen-share access is used to view/extract banking data, unauthorized access under Section 43 also applies.
punishment: Section 66C/66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh each. Section 66: up to 3 years and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh. Any resulting cheating under BNS 318 can extend punishment up to 7 years.

situation: I received a call from an actual TRAI customer helpline (which I called myself using the number from their official website) to ask a billing question.
explanation: Initiating contact with a genuine regulatory authority's verified helpline, found through their official website, for a legitimate query is normal and safe practice.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: A scammer created a fake customer support number for a popular e-commerce company and got it to rank high on search engines, so when I searched for the company's support number and called it, the fake agent convinced me to share my card details for a 'refund process.'
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: This is the 'fake customer care number' scam, where fraudsters exploit search engine optimization to plant fake support numbers that rank above genuine ones. Impersonating a legitimate company's customer support to extract financial information is cheating by personation through a computer resource under Section 66D, combined with identity theft under Section 66C.
punishment: Section 66C/66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh each. BNS cheating provisions under Section 318 can extend punishment based on amount defrauded.

situation: I called the customer support number listed directly on the back of my credit card or on the bank's official app to report a lost card.
explanation: Contacting customer support through a number sourced directly from the bank's own card or official app, rather than from a search engine, is the safest and intended way to reach genuine support and poses no risk of impersonation fraud.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: A fraudster cloned my company's official website pixel-for-pixel on a similar-looking domain and is using it to collect customer payment details, which never reach us.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: Creating a near-identical clone of a legitimate business's website (typosquatting/phishing) to deceive customers into submitting payment information is a clear case of cheating by personation through a computer resource under Section 66D, combined with identity theft under Section 66C for impersonating the brand's digital identity.
punishment: Section 66C/66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh each. BNS cheating provisions under Section 318 can extend punishment based on amount defrauded from victims.

situation: My company registered a new domain name that closely matches our brand name, having properly purchased and verified it through an accredited domain registrar.
explanation: Legitimately purchasing and registering a domain name through proper, accredited channels for one's own business is a normal, lawful business activity.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: An ex-employee who still had access to our company's shared cloud drive (because IT forgot to revoke it after his exit) logged in and downloaded sensitive financial spreadsheets two months after leaving.
ipc_sections: Section 408 (criminal breach of trust by employee, given prior employment relationship)
bns_sections: Section 316(3) BNS (criminal breach of trust by employee)
explanation: Even though the access credentials technically still worked due to an administrative oversight, the former employee no longer had actual authorization to access company systems after termination. Logging in and extracting sensitive data under these circumstances is unauthorized access under Sections 43 and 66 of the IT Act, since authorization is based on the employment relationship, not merely whether credentials happen to still function.
punishment: Section 66: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh. Criminal breach of trust under BNS 316(3) given the prior position of trust: up to 10 years imprisonment.

situation: I'm a current employee with active, authorized credentials, and I accessed our shared cloud drive to retrieve a report I need for tomorrow's client meeting, as part of my normal job duties.
explanation: Accessing company systems within the scope of one's current, authorized job role using valid credentials for legitimate work purposes is entirely normal and lawful employment activity.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: Someone created a deepfake audio clip of a company's CFO announcing fake bad news about the company to manipulate its stock price before short-selling it.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
ipc_sections: Read with SEBI regulations on market manipulation
bns_sections: Read with SEBI regulations on market manipulation
explanation: Creating fabricated audio impersonating a company executive to manipulate stock prices is a severe combination of cheating by personation under Section 66D of the IT Act and securities market manipulation, which is separately and heavily penalized under the SEBI Act, 1992, and related regulations given the systemic financial harm involved.
punishment: Section 66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh. SEBI Act violations for market manipulation can attract penalties up to Rs. 25 crore or three times the profit made, along with imprisonment up to 10 years under the SEBI Act.

situation: A financial analyst publicly shared their genuine, well-researched opinion that a company's stock is overvalued, based on publicly available financial filings.
explanation: Sharing a genuine, well-reasoned investment opinion based on publicly available information is normal financial commentary and analysis, protected as free expression, and is a routine part of financial markets discourse.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: A fraudulent caller, claiming to represent a popular electricity board, sent me an SMS saying my electricity will be disconnected tonight unless I update my billing details by clicking a link and entering my card information.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: This is a utility-bill phishing scam impersonating an electricity board to create urgency and extract payment card details. This is cheating by personation through a computer resource (SMS/link) under Section 66D, combined with identity theft under Section 66C.
punishment: Section 66C/66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh each.

situation: I paid my electricity bill through the utility provider's official mobile app or website, which I accessed directly by typing the official URL myself.
explanation: Paying a bill through the provider's official, verified channel that you accessed directly is normal, safe digital bill payment.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: A group of students used AI chatbots to generate someone else's entire college assignment and submitted it as their own original work without disclosure, violating their institution's academic integrity policy.
explanation: While this is a serious academic integrity violation that an institution may penalize through internal disciplinary action (such as grade penalties, suspension, or expulsion under its academic honesty code), it does not, by itself, constitute a criminal offence under the IT Act, IPC, or BNS, since there's no unauthorized access, fraud against a third party, or data theft involved - this is a matter of institutional policy enforcement.
punishment: Not applicable as a cybercrime - this is an academic integrity matter handled through institutional disciplinary processes, not criminal law.

situation: Someone hacked into a school's online portal and leaked the question papers for an upcoming board examination to students in exchange for payment.
explanation: Unauthorized access to a school's examination portal to steal and sell confidential question papers is a clear violation of Sections 43 and 66 of the IT Act (unauthorized access and data theft), combined with cheating under the BNS for selling the stolen material, and would also constitute an offence under applicable state anti-cheating/exam-leak legislation where such laws exist.
punishment: Section 66: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh. State-specific exam leak laws (where applicable) often carry significantly higher penalties, sometimes including life imprisonment for organized paper leaks.

situation: A scammer is impersonating a popular cryptocurrency exchange's official support account on Twitter/X (using a similar handle and logo) and replying to customer complaints with phishing links disguised as 'official support.'
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: This is a common 'fake support handle' scam targeting cryptocurrency users, where scammers monitor public complaints and respond with fake support links to phish credentials. This is identity theft (Section 66C) and cheating by personation through a computer resource (Section 66D).
punishment: Section 66C/66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh each.

situation: I contacted a cryptocurrency exchange's support through the verified, blue-checkmarked official account linked directly from their own website.
explanation: Reaching out through a verified official channel linked directly from the company's own legitimate website is the safe, intended way to get genuine support.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: A person created multiple fake LinkedIn profiles claiming to be recruiters from well-known companies to collect resumes, personal details, and bank account information from job seekers under the guise of processing 'joining formalities.'
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: Creating fake recruiter profiles impersonating real companies to harvest sensitive personal and financial information from job seekers under false pretenses is identity theft under Section 66C combined with cheating by personation through a computer resource under Section 66D.
punishment: Section 66C/66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh each. BNS cheating provisions can extend further if money was also extracted.

situation: A genuine HR recruiter from a company I applied to contacted me through LinkedIn using their verified profile, which matched the company's official employee directory, to schedule an interview.
explanation: Being contacted by a verifiable, genuine recruiter through professional channels for a legitimate interview process is normal job-search activity.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: Someone is running a fake charity fundraiser online, using real photos of disaster victims without their consent, to solicit donations that are never actually distributed to anyone affected.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
Section 66E (unauthorized use of victims' images, if applicable)
explanation: Operating a fraudulent charity campaign that uses real disaster imagery to dishonestly solicit and misappropriate donations is cheating committed via a computer resource under Section 66D of the IT Act, combined with cheating under BNS Section 318. If the victims' images were used without their consent, this also raises privacy concerns under Section 66E.
punishment: Section 66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh. BNS 318 (cheating): up to 7 years depending on amount collected and clause invoked.

situation: I donated to a disaster relief fundraiser run by a registered, well-established NGO with a transparent track record and proper tax-exemption certification.
explanation: Donating to a verified, registered charitable organization with established credibility and proper certification is a normal, lawful, and commendable act of charitable giving.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.

situation: A 'recovery agent' contacted me online claiming they can help recover money I previously lost in a different scam, in exchange for an upfront 'processing fee,' but this is itself a secondary scam targeting prior fraud victims.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
explanation: This is a recognized 'recovery scam' pattern that specifically re-targets previous fraud victims by promising to recover lost funds for an upfront fee, which is itself a fresh act of cheating committed via a computer resource under Section 66D of the IT Act and BNS Section 318.
punishment: Section 66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh. BNS 318 (cheating): up to 7 years depending on amount and clause invoked.

situation: After losing money to a scam, I filed a complaint through the official National Cybercrime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in) and the 1930 helpline to seek legitimate recovery assistance.
explanation: Reporting fraud through India's official, government-run cybercrime reporting channels is the correct, safe, and recommended course of action for any victim of online fraud.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out; this is the recommended remedial action for cybercrime victims.

situation: An online forex/stock trading 'guru' on Telegram promised to multiply my investment using 'insider trading signals' and 'guaranteed profit algorithms,' and after I invested through their app, I could see fake profits accumulating but couldn't withdraw any money.
it_act_sections: Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource)
ipc_sections: Read with SEBI regulations on unregistered investment advisory
bns_sections: Read with SEBI regulations on unregistered investment advisory
explanation: This is a 'pig butchering' style investment scam pattern, where a fake trading app displays fabricated profits to encourage further deposits, but withdrawals are blocked. This is cheating committed via a computer resource under Section 66D of the IT Act, and operating as an unregistered/unlicensed investment advisor separately violates SEBI regulations.
punishment: Section 66D: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh. BNS 318 (cheating): up to 7 years depending on amount and clause invoked. SEBI Act violations carry separate substantial penalties.

situation: I invest in mutual funds and stocks through a SEBI-registered broker using their official app, and I track my portfolio performance regularly.
explanation: Investing through a properly licensed, SEBI-registered broker via their official platform is standard, lawful, and regulated investment activity.
punishment: Not applicable - no offence is made out.
